slides.heading: Longest Peak
slides.subtitle: AlgoExpert · Medium · Arrays
slides.narration: Let's solve Longest Peak, a medium arrays problem. We'll restate the problem, build the intuition, walk through the approach, read the Java solution, and finish with its complexity.

slides.heading: The problem
bullets: Length of the longest strictly-increasing-then-strictly-decreasing run (needs >= 3 items).
slides.narration: Here's the problem. Length of the longest strictly-increasing-then-strictly-decreasing run (needs over equals 3 items).

slides.heading: Intuition
bullets: A peak is a strict rise then a strict fall, so find each tip and expand both ways.
slides.narration: A peak is a strict rise then a strict fall, so find each tip and expand both ways.

slides.heading: Brute force vs optimal
bullets: Brute force: from every index, expand a peak → O(n²)
Optimal: only expand from tips, skip past each peak → O(n)
Each element is visited at most twice
slides.narration: Expanding from every index is quadratic. Instead, only tips, values higher than both neighbours, can be peaks. Expanding from each tip and then jumping to the peak's end means each element is touched a constant number of times.

slides.heading: Approach
bullets: 1. Find indices higher than both neighbours
2. Expand left while values keep decreasing outward
slides.narration: Step by step. First, find indices higher than both neighbours. Second, expand left while values keep decreasing outward. Third, expand right likewise. Fourth, track the longest span.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: Tip 4 at 4 → peak spans 3…5 (length 3)
slides.narration: Index 4, value 4, is higher than both neighbours, so it's a tip. Expanding left while values fall and right while values fall gives a peak from 3 to 5, length 3.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: Tip 10 at 6 → peak spans 5…10 (length 6)
slides.narration: Index 6, value 10, is higher than both neighbours, so it's a tip. Expanding left while values fall and right while values fall gives a peak from 5 to 10, length 6.

slides.heading: Java solution
slides.narration: We scan from index one. When the current value is a tip, we walk l left while values keep increasing toward the tip and r right while they keep decreasing, update the best length, and jump i to r. Otherwise i moves on.

slides.heading: Complexity
slides.narration: Time is O of n. Space is constant.

slides.heading: Edge cases & pitfalls
bullets: Need ≥ 3 elements; only rising or only falling → 0
Jump i to r to avoid rescanning
slides.narration: Inequalities are strict, so a plateau breaks a peak. A purely increasing array has no peak and returns zero.

slides.heading: Interview tips & follow-ups
bullets: Draw the array as a mountain range while explaining
slides.narration: Sketching the values as a mountain range makes this easy to explain. Variants ask for the longest valley.

slides.heading: Recap
bullets: A peak is a strict rise then a strict fall, so find each tip and expand both ways.
slides.narration: To recap Longest Peak: A peak is a strict rise then a strict fall, so find each tip and expand both ways. Try re-implementing it from scratch without looking.
